messages.subject: Short data analyses
parts:
Hi Vincent and others, 

I have tried to analyze short data from a calibration study in Brazil. However, different from our previous experience, these are all short data and we are not able to use the old codes.
It is probably related to the calibration process, but my tries to change these arguments were not effectives.

Thanks in advance.

Inácio Crochemore M da Silva
Federal University of Pelotas

messages.author: 8d92e34685fbc6bd
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Short data analyses
parts:
Hi Inacio,
For experiments that last only a couple of hours you should adjust argument windowsizes to be meaningful relative to the duration of your experiment. For example, windowsizes = c(5, 300, 300), would require at least 5 minutes of data (300 seconds) as it attempts to do non-wear detection per 5 minute window.
Cheers, Vincent

messages.author: 8d92e34685fbc6bd
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Short data analyses
parts:
Inacio and Marcio,
If you have data from a lab experiment that last only a couple of hours then the auto-calibration may not be successful because there will be limited data for this algorithm to train on. Your calibration results should confirm this. In https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27878845 we addressed this by using free-living data for the autocalibration.

In that case you set do.cal = FALSE and use calibration coefficients as separate input.

ENMO is not produced because there is no enough monitor wear time in a day. I think it is more logical to work with the epoch level data that is produced by part 1 directly and not use part 2 (or 3, 4, 5) for analysing experimental data that lasts only a couple of hours.

Vincent

Hi Alex, Marcio, and Inacio,

I think I have addressed the issue now. It seems to have been related to the updates I made to the timestamp format in August 2016, which seems to have broken a few small parts of the code affecting versions 1.2-10 (August 2016) till version 1.3-2 (November 2016).

I just uploaded the fixed version 1.4 to CRAN, which normally be online in the upcoming 24 hours. Here is a link to the github version if you want to try it out sooner: https://github.com/ucl-cls/mcs-acc/releases/download/v1.4/GGIR_1.4.tar.gz

Best wishes and thanks for the feedback,
Vincent

On Sunday, January 22, 2017 at 3:24:28 PM UTC, Vincent van Hees wrote:

Hi Alex, Marcio, and Inacio,

I think I have addressed the issue now. It seems to have been related to the updates I made to the timestamp format in August 2016, which seems to have broken a few small parts of the code affecting versions 1.2-10 (August 2016) till version 1.3-2 (November 2016).

I just uploaded the fixed version 1.4 to CRAN, which normally be online in the upcoming 24 hours. Here is a link to the github version if you want to try it out sooner: https://github.com/ucl-cls/mcs-acc/releases/download/v1.4/GGIR_1.4.tar.gz

Vincent
On 18 January 2017 at 17:55, <alex.r...@unisa.edu.au> wrote:

Hi Vincent (and others),

I am also processing short lab files and trying to get the epoch values in csv. I have done this previously (mid 2016), but can't seem to get them now. 

I have set do.cal to FALSE and used calibration coefficients as separate input and am only using short window sizes (1,600,600). 

Part 1 has run fine and I have generated the meta files. However, I am unable to use the epochvalues2csv argument in g.part2 - I get an error message about missing the first midnight when I run part 2 (strategy 1, but I have tried all). I note you recommend only using part 1 when dealing with short data files, what's the best way to generate the csv epoch files from the meta files for these short lab files?

Any advice much appreciated.

Best,
Alex

On Wednesday, January 4, 2017 at 4:36:19 PM UTC, Vincent van Hees wrote:
Inacio and Marcio,
If you have data from a lab experiment that last only a couple of hours then the auto-calibration may not be successful because there will be limited data for this algorithm to train on. Your calibration results should confirm this. In https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27878845 we addressed this by using free-living data for the autocalibration.

In that case you set do.cal = FALSE and use calibration coefficients as separate input.

ENMO is not produced because there is no enough monitor wear time in a day. I think it is more logical to work with the epoch level data that is produced by part 1 directly and not use part 2 (or 3, 4, 5) for analysing experimental data that lasts only a couple of hours.

Vincent

Your calibration results should confirm this. In https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27878845 we addressed this by using free-living data for the autocalibration.

In that case you set do.cal = FALSE and use calibration coefficients as separate input.

ENMO is not produced because there is no enough monitor wear time in a day. I think it is more logical to work with the epoch level data that is produced by part 1 directly and not use part 2 (or 3, 4, 5) for analysing experimental data that lasts only a couple of hours.

Vincent

Hi Inacio,
For experiments that last only a couple of hours you should adjust argument windowsizes to be meaningful relative to the duration of your experiment. For example, windowsizes = c(5, 300, 300), would require at least 5 minutes of data (300 seconds) as it attempts to do non-wear detection per 5 minute window.
